Sunday, 25 June, morning, on the balcony. Rose-Hélène is asleep. Julien hasn’t slept all night. He finally tells Ioana about Olivier Marchand’s offer.
Ioana, I need to talk to you. Last night, after the concert, my former teacher offered me a post. At the Paris Conservatoire.
(puts down her cup) Paris? The Conservatoire? But Julien… it’s your dream! Why the long face?
Because the post starts in January. And I won’t leave without you two. I’ll only accept on condition that you really agree.
Wait. Let’s think calmly. In case we left, what would I do? The Fourvière room will be finished in September…
You’d find work in Paris. There are hundreds of architects’ firms. Unless you’d rather carry on remotely with Nathalie.
That’s just it… Nathalie told me on Friday she wanted to offer to make me her partner. After the inauguration. On condition that I stay in Lyon, of course.
(silence) Partner? Ioana, that’s fantastic. Why didn’t you tell me anything?
I wanted to wait until it was official. And you waited a whole night. We’re well matched.
Right. Let’s weigh up the pros and cons. Supposing we leave, we’d have to find a flat. Rents in Paris are twice as high.
And Rose-Hélène would change nursery, just after getting used to it. And Hélène… she’s eighty-six, Julien.
I know. But if I ever refuse, I’ll wonder all my life what would have happened.
Then don’t refuse straight away. Go to Paris, visit the Conservatoire, talk to your teacher. Unless you’ve already decided.
No. I’m not deciding anything without you. I could go on Thursday, provided Odile can look after the little one in the evening.
She’ll say yes, you know her. And Isabelle lives in Paris, doesn’t she? You could sleep at her place, in case you miss the last train.
You think of everything. (takes her hand) Let’s hope we make the right decision.

"Oh-ka-oo": the s in "cas" is silent. Stress on "où".
"A-so-see-ay": ss = voiceless s, the two "e"s at the end sound like one.
"Au cas où" (in case) is followed by the CONDITIONAL, not the subjunctive. It expresses a possibility you are preparing for:
In case we left, what would I do?
You could sleep at her place, in case you miss the train.
Take an umbrella, in case it rains.
Common mistake: "au cas où il pleuve" (subjunctive). Correct: "au cas où il PLEUVRAIT". And don’t use the future: "au cas où il pleuvra" is wrong.
Four conjunctions of condition require the SUBJUNCTIVE (ch. 25):
à condition que tu sois d’accord
à moins que tu ne préfères rester
pourvu que nous prenions la bonne décision
After "à moins que" a "ne" without negative meaning often appears (expletive ne): "à moins qu’il ne pleuve" = unless it rains. It’s elegant, but optional. Don’t add "pas"!
"Pourvu que" on its own at the start of a sentence expresses a wish: "Pourvu qu’il fasse beau !" = Let’s hope it’s nice!
3. Si jamais and sauf si + indicative
Like plain "si", these two expressions are followed by the INDICATIVE (present, imperfect…):
If I ever refuse, I’ll wonder all my life…
Go to Paris, unless you’ve already decided.
"Si jamais" is less likely than "si": it shows a possibility you don’t think is very certain.
When the subject is the same in both parts of the sentence, you use the preposition + INFINITIVE instead of "que" + subjunctive:
J’accepterai à condition que tu sois d’accord.
Nous partirons à moins qu’il ne pleuve.
Nous partirons à moins d’être malades.
si, si jamais, sauf si, même si
à condition que, à moins que, pourvu que, en supposant que
Trick: the ones with "que" take the subjunctive. "Au cas où" is the exception with the conditional. The ones with "si" take the indicative.
I’ll accept on condition that you agree.
We’ll go out, unless it rains.
Take your jacket in case it’s cold.
à moins qu’il ne soit trop tard
à moins qu’il n’est pas trop tard
à moins qu’il ne soit pas trop tard

On Thursday 29 June, Julien took the seven o’clock TGV from Part-Dieu station. Ioana had packed him a bag with a sandwich, a bottle of water, a jumper "in case it’s cold on the train" and a toothbrush, in case he missed the last train in the evening.

During the journey he watched the fields of Burgundy roll past without really seeing them. He had promised Ioana to look at Paris with fresh eyes, as if he were going to live there. "Don’t decide anything," she had told him on the platform. "Look, listen, and come back to me."

At nine he arrived at the Gare de Lyon. The metro was packed; a man trod on his foot without apologising, a woman was reading a novel while holding the rail with one hand. Julien thought that if he came to live here, he would make this journey twice a day.

The Conservatoire was in the north-east of the city, in a large modern building next to a park. Olivier Marchand was waiting for him at the entrance. He showed him the classrooms, the recording studios, the library, and the great concert hall, where a student orchestra was rehearsing Ravel.

Julien stopped at the door and listened for a long time. He had been twenty when he first dreamed of this hall. He had sat the entrance exam, long ago, and had failed by two points. That was when he had decided to become a teacher.

At noon, Marchand took him to lunch at a little restaurant by the canal. He explained the details of the post: twelve hours of teaching a week, students aged twenty to thirty from all over the world, and a salary almost twice as high as in Lyon. "On condition that you’re here on 5 January, of course."

Then, over coffee, Marchand added something strange. "I’ll be honest with you, Julien. In case Paris doesn’t suit you, you should know that my colleague in Lyon is preparing something too. But I’m not allowed to say more. And it wouldn’t be for another year."

In the afternoon, Julien visited three flats, as Ioana had asked him to. The first, a thirty-five-square-metre two-room flat on the fifth floor with no lift, cost one thousand six hundred euros a month. The bedroom was so small that a cot wouldn’t fit, unless you put the bed in the kitchen.

The second was bigger, but it looked onto a boulevard where cars honked day and night. The third was perfect: bright, quiet, with a little balcony. The agent smiled. "There are forty applicants. If by any chance you’re interested, you’d have to sign today." Julien thanked him and left.

Meanwhile, in Lyon, Ioana had left the office early to go up to Fourvière. She needed to talk to someone, and she knew exactly who. Hélène was in the garden, under the lime tree, a book on her knees. She understood at once, just from seeing Ioana’s face.

Ioana told her everything: the Paris offer, Nathalie’s, the two columns of her list, perfectly equal. Hélène listened without interrupting. Then she closed her book and looked for a long time at the city below, with its red roofs and its two rivers.

"You know, my dear," she said at last, "Henri left alone. He didn’t ask my opinion. He decided for both of us, and he was wrong. The worst thing isn’t leaving, or staying. The worst thing is deciding alone."

"But you," she added, taking her hand, "are not alone. As long as you stay together, Paris or Lyon doesn’t matter much. And don’t stay for my sake. I’m eighty-six. As long as you’re happy, I’ll be happy. Even from afar."

Ioana cried a little. Hélène handed her an embroidered handkerchief, very old, with an H in one corner. "It’s the last one my mother embroidered for my trousseau," she said. "I never married, so I used them all for crying. Keep this one."

In Paris, in the evening, Julien had dinner at Isabelle’s, Odile’s daughter, in her flat in the eleventh arrondissement. She worked at a publishing house and lived alone with two cats. She had left Lyon at twenty-five, after her wedding, and had stayed after her divorce.

"I don’t regret Paris," she said, pouring the wine. "Everything is here. But I miss Mum every day. I see her four times a year, and each time I find she has aged. If you ever come, come for the music. Not for the prestige. Prestige doesn’t keep you warm at night."

They talked for so long that Julien missed the last train, exactly as Ioana had predicted. Isabelle made him a bed on the sofa, between the two cats, who watched him suspiciously all night. Julien took the toothbrush out of the bag and smiled.

At midnight he called Ioana. She wasn’t asleep either. They talked in whispers, like two teenagers. She told him about her visit to Hélène, the handkerchief, the sentence about Henri. He told her about the concert hall, the orchestra, the restaurant, the overpriced flats, the suspicious cats.

"So?" asked Ioana. "Did you see Paris with fresh eyes?" Julien thought. "I saw a magnificent city," he said. "A concert hall I dreamed about for fifteen years. But on every street corner I wondered what you would think of it. And I had no one to tell."

"And the flats?" asked Ioana, half laughing. "Did you find our future palace?" Julien described the two-room flat on the fifth floor, the bedroom too small for a cot, the noisy boulevard, the agent and his forty applicants. "In case we came," he concluded, "Rose-Hélène would sleep in the bathtub. And we’d miss Victor terribly."

There was a long silence. Then Julien added: "There’s something else. Marchand said a strange thing at lunch. Something being prepared in Lyon. He wouldn’t tell me more." Ioana asked what. "I don’t know," Julien replied. "But I intend to find out."

After hanging up, Ioana sat for a long time in the dark, Hélène’s handkerchief in her hand. In the cot, Rose-Hélène was sleeping with her arms above her head. Victor, who had come over from Odile’s via the balcony, had settled at her feet, as if standing guard.

Ioana picked up her list again and added a line at the bottom, under the two columns, in capital letters: "Decide nothing alone." Then she switched off the lamp. For the first time in five days, she fell asleep straight away.

That night, Ioana makes a list of pros and cons. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
It’s two in the morning. Julien is finally asleep. I can’t manage it. So I took a sheet of paper and drew two columns: "for" and "against".
For: it’s Julien’s dream. If he refuses, he’ll regret it, unless he finds another dream in Lyon. Paris is a magnificent city, full of museums and concerts.
Against: my job. Nathalie is offering to make me a partner, on condition that I stay here. You only get a chance like that once in your life.
Against: our Lyon family. Hélène, Odile, Radu and Lucia, Karim and Leïla. In case we left, who would look after the little one on Wednesdays? Who would visit Hélène?
For: Paris is only two hours by train. Supposing we came back every other weekend, we wouldn’t lose anyone. Unless we’re lying to ourselves.
I looked at my list for a long time. The two columns are exactly the same length. Let’s hope Paris helps us choose on Thursday. Otherwise, I’ll toss a coin.
